data.title: Why Silver Investors Are Paying Attention To What’s Happening At Alamos
data.description:
Key points

  • In October 2026, drilling intersected the high-grade Africa blind vein (669 g/t AgEq over 2.05 m), proving that unmined silver structures with zero surface indicators sit parallel to the 26 known veins at Alamos.

  • Unlike most early-stage explorers, Minaurum Silver (TSXV:MGG) already holds underground mining approval (MIA) in Mexico, which allows new discoveries to share existing infrastructure.

  • Through the rehabilitation of 600+ m of historic colonial tunnels and extending drill holes where warranted, management is compounding its resource scale ahead of a scheduled update without the buildout costs.

  • As a pre-revenue junior player (CA$78M-CA$91M market cap), Minaurum relies on equity markets to fund drilling and still must prove vein continuity.

Traditional silver investors typically see early-stage mining as a black box of technical jargon. But when we strip away the geology, the business logic looks more similar than you’d expect.

Take commercial real estate as an example. The best returns rarely come from buying unzoned land in the middle of nowhere (unless you’re a data center), they come from discovering untapped square footage on a property that’s already zoned, permitted and connected to the grid.

In mining, a “blind” vein is much the same. It’s a high-grade deposit of silver that never broke through to the earth’s surface, trampled over by surface prospectors for centuries who never suspected it was there.

For the uninitiated, “AgEq”, or silver equivalent, is the accounting shorthand used to evaluate secondary metals found in the same rock (gold, copper, lead etc) into a single, simple grade.

Silver’s demand

Silver is a hot commodity with a demand problem, used for solar panel, grid electrification and AI data center hardware manufacturing.

Finding projects with existing permits and near-term development paths is tough, especially while many junior exploration companies burn shareholder cash chasing unpermitted projects from scratch.

Enter Minaurum

On October 22, Vancouver-based Minaurum struck silver and demonstrated its sharp capital-allocation methodology at the Alamos Silver Project in Sonora, Mexico. A project it owns outright.

While drilling a known zone called “Europa Sur” during its 50,000 m Phase II expansion, company geologists spotted subtle changes in the surrounding rock continuing past their planned target depth.

Rather than shutting it down to save on drilling, the team kept going.

The hidden vein silver investors should know about

Roughly 50 m off to the side of their main target, Hole AL26-268 (for the non-miners: “AL” = Alamos, “26” = 2026 and “268” = the 268th hole drilled) intersected 2.05 m grading 669 g/t AgEq.

Composed of 270 g/t pure silver alongside gold, copper, lead and zinc credits, it follows Hole AL26-257, which cut 1.30 m of 592 g/t AgEq.

This newly named “Africa vein zone” lines up roughly 400 m away with a 2019 drill hole (AL19-018), leading to the hypothesis that a parallel deposit was hiding right next to the company’s existing footprint.

Asset and catalyst snapshot

  • Footprint

100%-owned, 37,928-hectare district with an initial resource of 55.2 Moz AgEq (320 g/t AgEq; 34.8 Moz pure silver) modeled across only 3 of 26 known vein zones.

  • The blind vein

The new Africa vein hit 2.05 m of 669 g/t AgEq and 1.30 m of 592 g/t AgEq ~50 m away from Europa Sur.

  • Broader hits

High-grade step-outs outside the initial resource at:

  • Europa Sur: 0.60 m of 1,140 g/t AgEq; 2.65 m of 367 g/t AgEq

  • Quintera: 1.50 m of 462 g/t AgEq

  • San Jose: 0.30 m of 782 g/t AgEq

  • Regulatory moat

Minaurum holds full MIA underground mining permits, the only recent production-permitted silver discovery in Mexico.

What the 17th-century miners left behind

Silver mining in Alamos dates back to 1683, underwriting centuries of colonial architecture until groundwater and the Mexican Revolution halted work around 1911.

Today, the historic Promontorio workings are where Minaurum has restored over 600 m of haulage tunnels. Geologists still walk past hand-chiseled stopes and a stone prayer altar carved into the wall from its initial discovery centuries ago.

Led by CEO Darrell Rader and VP of Exploration Stephen Maynard, Minaurum has turned that century-old footprint into a modern advantage.

Rather than proposing the traditional open-pit mine in a heritage town, the company designed an underground operation using the existing architecture. Which in turn earned community support and helped the firm secure full underground mining permits ahead of its expansion.

Why it matters for silver investors

Like any mining resource, silver wears a couple of hats: serving as a financial hedge and an industrial component. This dual role gives silver investments strong upside during supply squeezes, but can punish companies that burn cash on slow, dilutive builds.

Think back to the real estate analogy. True asymmetric upside comes from finding high-grade zones on already-permitted infrastructure, not paying for permits and construction costs twice.

Due to its proximity, the Africa vein could share future underground access and processing infrastructure for Minaurum, lowering capital intensity per ounce.

In this instance, there are three key signals that separate Minaurum from other speculative drillers:

  1. Permits

Core environmental and operating approvals, such as Mexico’s MIA permit, are secured before major expansion capital is used.

  1. Field agility

Technical teams have the resourcing and capability to extend holes when rock alteration warrants it, just as Minaurum did with Hole AL26-257.

  1. Multi-asset cushions

Gold, copper, lead and zinc credits help buffer margins when silver prices swing. Which it’s been known to do.

Operational risks and market realities

Despite the permit moat and drill momentum, commodities can always be volatile and Minaurum still carries the real-world risks of a pre-revenue junior developer including:

  • Equity dilution

It trades at around CA$0.19 to CA$0.22 per share throughout November 2026 and has a sub-CA$100M market cap. The firm generates no operating revenue and relies on equity markets to fund drilling and engineering.

  • Vein continuity risk

Narrow underground veins can pinch and swell necessitating tighter drill spacing to confirm mineable widths in the upcoming resource model.

  • Commodity and jurisdictional exposure

Economics remain sensitive to silver and base-metal price swings as well as regulatory consistency in Mexico.

As Minaurum folds the Africa blind vein into its updated resource estimate, the takeaway for investors is clear: when the silver market’s tight, the most valuable ounces are often hiding right beside infrastructure you already have permission to mine.

data.title: Just Four Days Till SLB N.V. (NYSE:SLB) Will Be Trading Ex-Dividend
data.description:
Some investors rely on dividends for growing their wealth, and if you're one of those dividend sleuths, you might be intrigued to know that SLB N.V. (NYSE:SLB) is about to go ex-dividend in just four days. The ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the cut-off date for shareholders to be present on the company's books to be eligible for a dividend payment. The ex-dividend date is of consequence because whenever a stock is bought or sold, the trade takes at least one business day to settle. Therefore, if you purchase SLB's shares on or after the 2nd of December, you won't be eligible to receive the dividend, when it is paid on the 7th of January.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$0.295 per share. Last year, in total, the company distributed US$1.18 to shareholders. Calculating the last year's worth of payments shows that SLB has a trailing yield of 2.4% on the current share price of US$48.52. If you buy this business for its dividend, you should have an idea of whether SLB's dividend is reliable and sustainable. That's why we should always check whether the dividend payments appear sustainable, and if the company is growing.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Dividends are typically paid from company earnings. If a company pays more in dividends than it earned in profit, then the dividend could be unsustainable. SLB paid out more than half (56%) of its earnings last year, which is a regular payout ratio for most companies. That said, even highly profitable companies sometimes might not generate enough cash to pay the dividend, which is why we should always check if the dividend is covered by cash flow. It distributed 45% of its free cash flow as dividends, a comfortable payout level for most companies.

It's encouraging to see that the dividend is covered by both profit and cash flow. This generally suggests the dividend is sustainable, as long as earnings don't drop precipitously.

Check out our latest analysis for SLB

Click here to see the company's payout ratio, plus analyst estimates of its future dividends.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Stocks in companies that generate sustainable earnings growth often make the best dividend prospects, as it is easier to lift the dividend when earnings are rising. Investors love dividends, so if earnings fall and the dividend is reduced, expect a stock to be sold off heavily at the same time. With that in mind, we're encouraged by the steady growth at SLB, with earnings per share up 7.2% on average over the last five years. Decent historical earnings per share growth suggests SLB has been effectively growing value for shareholders. However, it's now paying out more than half its earnings as dividends. Therefore it's unlikely that the company will be able to reinvest heavily in its business, which could presage slower growth in the future.

The main way most investors will assess a company's dividend prospects is by checking the historical rate of dividend growth. SLB's dividend payments per share have declined at 5.1% per year on average over the past 10 years, which is uninspiring. It's unusual to see earnings per share increasing at the same time as dividends per share have been in decline. We'd hope it's because the company is reinvesting heavily in its business, but it could also suggest business is lumpy.

To Sum It Up

Is SLB worth buying for its dividend? Earnings per share growth has been modest and SLB paid out over half of its profits and less than half of its free cash flow, although both payout ratios are within normal limits. In summary, while it has some positive characteristics, we're not inclined to race out and buy SLB today.

While it's tempting to invest in SLB for the dividends alone, you should always be mindful of the risks involved. Every company has risks, and we've spotted 2 warning signs for SLB you should know about.
